lesson_title: Simple and Compound Events: Trees, Grids and the Minibus You Watched
hook_text: Toss a coin twice. 'Three outcomes, so a third each,' says half the class. The tree diagram says they just lost the mark.
clip_script: Coin game at the fair: two tails wins a koeksister. Half the class says three outcomes — two tails, two heads, one of each — so a third each. Wrong, and here is the proof. Draw the tree. First toss: heads or tails. Second toss: branch again. FOUR journeys: heads-heads, heads-tails, tails-heads, tails-tails — a quarter each. 'One of each' is secretly TWO journeys sharing a name. That hidden twin, tails-heads, is the mark everyone drops. Two tails? One journey. One quarter. Now the minibus. No tree tells you if the 06:45 is full — so you watch. Full on 18 of 50 mornings: 18 over 50, that's 0,36. An estimate, and it sharpens the longer you watch. Coins get theory; minibuses get tallies. Last trick: hear 'at least one tail'? Don't add three branches. Flip it — the only failure is NO tails, one quarter — so 1 minus a quarter: three quarters. One line. Draw the tree, count the world, and chance stops being luck.
visual_style: A coin spinning in slow motion over a fair stall, branching into a glowing tree of four journeys with the forgotten tails-heads branch flashing; a minibus tally sheet filling morning by morning; the words AT LEAST ONE flipping over to reveal NONE.
mood: Playful but exacting — the friend who wins the fair games because they counted first.
pacing: Quick setup, a freeze on the wrong 'third each' answer, satisfying slow reveal of the four journeys, brisk through the minibus tally to the complement flip.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count your chances before you spend your ticket.
